dtz.lead: France asks for a proven level of French at each step: for a first multi-year card, a first resident card and naturalisation (to verify). The TCF IRN is the test made for this. Here you can read about it and practise with our own mock.
dtz.who.title: Who is this for?
dtz.who.text: The TCF IRN (Test de connaissance du français pour l'intégration, la résidence et la nationalité) is run by France Éducation international and taken at approved centres. As far as we could check, it can be used to show the French level asked for a residence card or for naturalisation, and the level you need depends on the step: A2, B1 or B2 (to verify). Some people are exempt, and other tests or diplomas may count instead. The rules change, so check the official sources before you book. This is general orientation, not legal advice. We are not affiliated with France Éducation international.
dtz.format.note: This is the structure of our own mock, not of the real TCF IRN: the real test has its own parts, number of questions and timings, which we have not copied and which are to verify on the official site. See also our TCF overview. The mock has no speaking part: practise that with our speaking tasks. The extra reading & writing tasks are good for more practice.
dtz.scoring.title: How the TCF IRN reports your result
dtz.scoring.text: As far as we could check, the TCF IRN gives you a level on the European scale (CEFR) for each skill, and the certificate is valid for a limited time (to verify the exact rules). In our mock the point bands are our own guide, not a TCF score or level.
dtz.set.title: Our TCF IRN mock: listening, reading and writing
dtz.set.text: Nine parts, 45 scored tasks in French between A2 and B1 (set 1) and B1 and B2 (set 2): listening parts 1–4 and reading parts 1–5, plus a writing task with a model answer. You can run a clock for each skill. At the end you see your result by part, with our own point bands as a guide. Progress stays saved in the browser.

dtz.mock.text: All four reading tasks as one continuous test at level B1, with an overall result at the end.

telc.lead: TCF-style tasks, one band at a time. The real TCF (tout public, IRN and Canada) is one test whose questions get harder as you go; here you can practise the tasks that aim at your level, band by band.

telc.who.title: Who is the TCF for?
telc.who.text: The TCF (Test de connaissance du français) is run by France Éducation international. It is one test for all levels rather than one exam per level, and it gives a level, not a pass or a fail. The TCF tout public is for study and work, the TCF IRN is for residence and nationality procedures in France, and the TCF Canada is for Canadian immigration. Which version you need, and which level, depends on the institution or procedure, so check before you book (to verify).
telc.sprachbausteine.note: The TCF tout public also has a compulsory paper on language structures (structures de la langue), and its writing and speaking papers are optional in some versions (to verify). Our sets hold the four skills. For grammar and vocabulary in context, use the language-in-use trainer below.
telc.moreLevels.title: How this differs from the real test
telc.moreLevels.text: The bands are our way of cutting up one test: you can't book a "TCF B1". Our tasks follow the kinds of task the TCF is known for, but numbers of questions, timings and word counts are our own and the real ones may differ (to verify). Check the current details with France Éducation international or your test centre.

goethe.lead: The official French diplomas of France's Ministry of Education: the DELF from A1 to B2 and the DALF at C1 and C2, recognised by employers, universities and public bodies.
goethe.practiceHeading: Practise for the DELF and DALF
goethe.who.title: Who are the DELF and DALF for?
goethe.who.text: Each DELF or DALF diploma is a separate exam for one level: DELF A1, A2, B1 and B2, then DALF C1 and C2. People use them for work, for study and, in some procedures, for a residence card or French nationality (which test and level an office asks for changes, so check with the office; see our residence and nationality page). As far as we could check, a diploma has no expiry date, though some institutions may ask for a recent result. To verify.

testdaf.who.text: The TEF (Test d'évaluation de français) is run by CCI Paris Île-de-France and taken at approved centres. TEF Canada is the version accepted for Canadian immigration and citizenship procedures. People also take the TEF for study and work, and a version for residence and nationality in France exists (to verify). grammatik.artikel.intro: French has le, la and l' for “the” in the singular, and les in the plural. For “a” it has un and une, and des for “some”. The article shows if the noun is masculine or feminine, singular or plural.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: Say a statement with your voice going up: Tu viens ? Or put est-ce que in front: Est-ce que tu viens ? Answer with oui or non. If the question is negative and your answer is yes, say si: Tu ne viens pas ? – Si !
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: The question word can go at the end: Tu habites où ? Or at the start with est-ce que: Où est-ce que tu habites ? Both are normal. The third way, Où habites-tu ?, is formal: you need to recognise it.
grammatik.praesens.intro: Most French verbs end in -er. Take off -er and add the ending for the person: parler → je parle, tu parles, nous parlons, vous parlez. Je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent all sound the same.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: Two more groups of regular verbs. -ir verbs like finir add -iss- in the plural: je finis, nous finissons. -re verbs like vendre, attendre and répondre have no ending in the il form: je vends, il vend.
grammatik.konjugation.intro: Some very common French verbs do not follow the rules: aller, faire, venir, prendre, mettre, voir, dire. Learn them whole: je vais, je fais, je viens, je prends, je mets, je vois, je dis.
grammatik.plural.intro: In writing, add -s: une maison → des maisons. Words in -eau and -eu add -x (un gâteau → des gâteaux), and words in -al change to -aux (un journal → des journaux). The -s is silent, so in speech the article les or des shows the plural.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? Mon appartement, ta clé, ses enfants. The possessive agrees with the thing you have, not with the owner: sa voiture can be his car or her car. For an owner's name, use de: la voiture de Karim.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: The imperative gives an order, an instruction or a piece of advice, with no subject: Mange ! (tu), Mangeons ! (nous), Mangez ! (vous). With tu, -er verbs lose their -s. Pronouns follow the verb with a hyphen: Donne-le-moi. Prends-le.
grammatik.aduso.intro: Use et (and), ou (or), mais (but) and parce que (because) to join words and sentences. Before il, elle, on or a vowel, parce que becomes parce qu': parce qu'il pleut. Use aussi and non plus for “also” and “not either”: Moi aussi. Moi non plus.
grammatik.nomen.intro: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a street. Endings help: -tion and -té are usually feminine (la station, la liberté), -ment and -age are usually masculine (le logement, le village). Learn each noun with le or la, or with un or une.
grammatik.komposita.intro: Être en train de + infinitive says that something is happening right now: Je suis en train de manger. Venir de + infinitive says that something has just happened: Elle vient de partir. Together with aller + infinitive (Je vais partir) you can speak about before, during and just after.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Each word does a job in the sentence. Knowing the job helps you use the word: a noun has a gender (le or la), a verb changes for the person (je parle, nous parlons), an adjective matches its noun (un sac noir, une robe noire).
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: The direct object (COD) is the person or thing the verb acts on, with no preposition. The pronouns me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les go before the conjugated verb: Je vois Ana. → Je la vois. Before a vowel: m', t', l'.
grammatik.dativ.intro: With verbs like parler à, téléphoner à or écrire à, the person after à becomes a small pronoun before the verb: me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Je parle à Léa → Je lui parle. J'écris à mes parents → Je leur écris.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: To say what you can, want, must or know how to do, use a conjugated verb + an infinitive: Je peux venir lundi. Elle veut changer de médecin. Nous devons partir. The second verb never changes. Il faut + infinitive says what has to be done.
grammatik.negation.intro: Put ne … pas around the verb: Je ne parle pas allemand. Before a vowel, ne becomes n': Je n'habite pas ici. After a negative verb, un, une, des and du become de: Je n'ai pas de voiture.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: Use the passé composé to say what happened and is finished: J'ai mangé à midi. Hier, nous avons travaillé. It is avoir (present) + a participle: j'ai fini, tu as vu, elle a pris. In the negative, ne … pas goes around avoir: Je n'ai pas mangé.
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: Use du, de la, de l' or des for "some" of something you eat, drink or cannot count: Je mange du pain. Je bois de l'eau. After a negative, and after quantities, only de or d' is left: Je ne mange pas de viande. Il y a beaucoup de monde. For likes and dislikes, use le, la, les: J'aime le café.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Use à with a city (à Paris), en with feminine countries and countries that start with a vowel (en France, en Iran), au with masculine countries (au Maroc) and aux with plural ones (aux États-Unis). French uses the same word for "in" and "to". To say where you come from, use de, d', du or des: Je viens du Maroc.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: With some French verbs the thing is the subject and the person is the indirect object: Tu me manques means I miss you. Ce quartier me plaît means I like this neighbourhood. Il me faut un justificatif means I need a proof, and Il me reste dix euros means I have ten euros left.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Many French verbs take a fixed preposition, usually à or de: penser à, s'intéresser à, réussir à, avoir besoin de, essayer de, s'occuper de. Some take none where English has one: attendre le bus, chercher un travail. Learn the verb and its preposition together.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: To talk about plans and the near future, use aller (present) + infinitive: Je vais appeler le médecin. Demain, nous allons déménager. Only aller changes. The second verb stays in the infinitive.
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: Some verbs form the passé composé with être, not avoir: aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir and all reflexive verbs. The participle then agrees with the subject: Elle est allée à la banque. Ils sont partis. Elle s'est levée.
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: Use quand for something that is sure to happen or for a moment in time: Quand j'aurai mon visa, je partirai. Use si for a condition that may or may not be true: Si tu viens, je serai content. Watch the tenses: quand + futur, but si + présent (never si + futur).
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: Use the imparfait for habits in the past and for descriptions: Quand j'étais petit, nous habitions à Lyon. Il faisait beau. Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Only être is different: j'étais.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: To avoid repeating a noun, use a possessive pronoun: Mon appartement est petit. Et le tien ? It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: Léa cherche ses clés, Karim cherche les siennes. To say who owns something, use c'est à moi or c'est le mien.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: Most French adjectives come after the noun: une voiture bleue, un collègue français. A few short, common ones come before: un petit appartement, une bonne idée. Some change their meaning with the position: un grand homme is a great man, un homme grand is a tall man.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: Add -ment to the feminine form of an adjective to make an adverb: lente → lentement, heureuse → heureusement. Adverbs describe a verb: Il parle lentement. Adjectives describe a noun: C'est un bon médecin, but Il travaille bien.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: Ordinals are the number + -ième: deuxième, troisième, cinquième. Only 1 is special: premier, première. Dates use normal numbers, except the 1st: le 2 mai, but le 1er mai. Floors: au rez-de-chaussée, au premier étage, au deuxième étage.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From 0 to 1000. 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71 use et: vingt et un, soixante et onze, but vingt-deux. 70 is soixante-dix, 80 is quatre-vingts (4 × 20) and 90 is quatre-vingt-dix. Cent and vingt take an -s only at the end: deux cents, but deux cent trois.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: An adjective agrees with its noun: add -e for feminine and -s for plural (un garçon content, une fille contente, des filles contentes). Most adjectives come after the noun (une voiture rouge), but a few short common ones come before it (un petit café, une bonne idée).
grammatik.gern.intro: In French the person who likes is the subject: j'aime le café, elle adore les chats. With a noun, always use the article (le, la, les): J'aime le café, never J'aime café. After the verb you can also use an infinitive: j'aime cuisiner.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: Être (to be) and avoir (to have) are the two most important French verbs, and both are irregular: Je suis infirmière. J'ai deux enfants. French uses avoir for age and many feelings: J'ai 30 ans. J'ai faim.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Use il y a for “there is / there are”: Il y a une pharmacie ici. Use c'est / ce sont to name someone or something: C'est mon frère. Use il est / elle est with a job alone: Il est médecin. With an article: C'est un bon médecin.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: To ask politely, don't say Je veux. Say Je voudrais un rendez-vous or J'aimerais prendre rendez-vous. To ask someone to do something: Pourriez-vous répéter ? or Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: The subjonctif présent is used after que in many everyday sentences: Il faut que je parte. Je veux que tu viennes. Take the ils form of the present, drop -ent and add -e, -es, -e, -ent; nous and vous keep the imparfait endings: que nous venions, que vous veniez. A few common verbs are irregular, for example être (que je sois) and avoir (que j'aie).
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: Both tenses talk about the past, but they do different jobs. The passé composé tells what happened, step by step: Hier, j'ai attendu une heure. The imparfait paints the background and the habits: Il pleuvait et il y avait du monde. Together they make a story: Je faisais la queue quand mon téléphone a sonné.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: To ask a question inside a sentence, drop est-ce que and the inversion, and use a normal word order: Je me demande si tu viens. Yes/no questions take si. Qu'est-ce que becomes ce que, qu'est-ce qui becomes ce qui. Où, quand, comment, pourquoi and combien stay the same: Dites-moi où vous habitez.
grammatik.passiv.intro: The passive is être + past participle, in the tense of the active verb, and the participle agrees with the subject: Votre demande a été enregistrée. Le dossier sera transmis à la préfecture. The agent comes with par, or with de after feelings and states: aimé de tous, couvert de neige. In everyday French, on, the pronominal passive (Ça se dit) and se faire + infinitive are often more natural than the passive.
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Celui, celle, ceux and celles replace a noun you have just named: Mon dossier est plus complet que celui de Karim. They are never used alone. They need de, qui, que or -ci / -là after them: celui de Léa, celle qui arrive, ceux que j'ai vus, celui-ci ou celui-là ?
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: French builds many nouns from verbs and adjectives with endings. The ending tells you the gender: la location, la décision, la sécurité are feminine; le paiement, le chauffage, le logement are masculine. Prefixes such as re-, dé- and in- change the meaning: refaire, défaire, impossible.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: If something started in the past and is still going on, French uses the present tense: J'habite ici depuis 2020. Il y a plus a period and a past tense means ago: Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans. Pendant says how long something lasted, en how long it took, and dans when it will happen counted from now.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: When the person who wants, feels or fears is the same as the person who acts, French uses the infinitive: Je veux partir. Je suis content de venir. When the people are different, it uses que and the subjunctive: Je veux que tu partes. Never say Je veux que je parte.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: Use the conditionnel for polite wishes and requests, advice, and what you would do: Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous. Pourriez-vous m'aider ? À ta place, j'irais voir un avocat. Take the stem of the futur (je parlerai, j'irai) and add the endings of the imparfait: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: For an imaginary situation now, use si + imparfait with the conditionnel présent: Si j'avais plus de temps, je ferais du sport. For something that did not happen in the past, use si + plus-que-parfait with the conditionnel passé: Si j'avais su, je serais venu. The two can be mixed: Si j'avais accepté ce poste, je vivrais à Lyon aujourd'hui. Never put the conditionnel after si.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Qui is the subject: la collègue qui travaille avec moi. Que (qu') is the object: le dossier que j'ai envoyé. Où gives a place or a time: la ville où j'habite, le jour où je suis arrivé. Dont replaces de + noun: le dossier dont j'ai besoin.
grammatik.irgend.intro: n'importe + a question word means "any … at all, it makes no difference": n'importe qui, n'importe quoi, n'importe où, n'importe quand, n'importe comment. Appelle-moi n'importe quand. Before a noun use n'importe quel / quelle, and as a pronoun n'importe lequel / laquelle. n'importe quoi can also mean "nonsense": Il dit n'importe quoi. For someone specific but unknown, use quelqu'un instead.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: The gérondif is en + the -ant form. It says when or how something happens: Je l'ai vu en sortant. C'est en pratiquant qu'on progresse. Its subject is the same as the subject of the main verb. The participe présent without en is mostly written and never agrees (les candidats ayant un diplôme), unlike the verbal adjective, which agrees (des enfants souriants).
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Replace pas in ne … pas to say more: Je ne travaille plus ici (not any more). Il ne vient jamais (never). Je ne vois rien (nothing). Je ne connais personne (nobody). After them, un, une and des become de: Je n'ai plus de pain.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: French has fixed verb + noun pairs that you must learn as a unit: prendre une décision, prendre rendez-vous, faire attention, faire la queue, poser une question, porter plainte, rendre service. The verb is often not the English one: you take a decision (not make one), and passer un examen means to take an exam, not to pass it. To pass, say réussir un examen.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: With être, the past participle agrees with the subject: Elle est partie. With avoir, it never agrees with the subject, but it agrees with a direct object placed before the verb: la lettre que j'ai écrite, je les ai vues. Reflexive verbs agree when the pronoun is the direct object (Elle s'est lavée) but not when it is indirect or when a direct object follows (Elle s'est lavé les mains). A participle can also be an adjective: une porte fermée.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: When there is no noun before the relative word, French uses ce: ce qui (subject), ce que (object), ce dont (verbs with de). Ce que je cherche, c'est un appartement calme. Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de temps. For emphasis, finish with c'est: Ce qui est important, c'est la santé. Le plus important, c'est la santé.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: Opinion verbs take the indicative when you are sure and the subjunctive when you doubt or deny: Je pense que Hugo a raison, but Je ne pense pas que Hugo ait raison. The same split works for expressions: Il est évident que tu as raison (indicative) against Il est possible que tu aies raison (subjunctive). Douter que always takes the subjunctive.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: For a condition that is real or likely, use si with the présent, and put the présent, the futur simple or the impératif in the main clause: Si tu viens, je préparerai le dîner. Si vous avez un problème, appelez-moi. Never use the futur after si. Before il and ils, si becomes s'il and s'ils, but not before elle or on.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: Bien que and quoique (although) take the subjunctive: Bien qu'il fasse froid, nous sortons. Même si (even if) takes the indicative, and malgré takes a noun. For a result, use si or tellement + adjective + que with the indicative: Il était si fatigué qu'il s'est endormi. Sans que and de sorte que (purpose) take the subjunctive.
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: After a reporting verb in the present, the tenses stay the same: Il dit qu'il vient. After a past reporting verb, they shift back: Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain. Commands become de + infinitive (Il m'a demandé de rappeler) and questions use si, ce que, ce qui or où, without inversion. Pronouns, possessives and time words change too.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: The plus-que-parfait is the past of the past: it names an action that was already finished before another past moment. Form it with the imparfait of avoir or être and the participle: Quand je suis arrivé, le film avait déjà commencé. Use it for explanations (parce qu'il avait oublié son badge), for regrets (Si seulement j'avais su !) and in reported speech.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: Many daily-routine verbs need a small pronoun that matches the subject: je me lève, tu te laves, elle s'habille. In the dictionary the verb starts with se: se lever. The pronoun goes right before the verb.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: Give a reason with parce que (after the main idea) or comme (at the start). Give a result with donc or alors. To say what you think or what someone says, use que: Je pense que c'est fermé. Il dit qu'il vient demain.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: Compare with plus, moins or aussi + adjective + que: Ce train est plus rapide que le bus. For "the most", put le, la or les in front: C'est la ville la plus chère. Bon becomes meilleur and bien becomes mieux, never plus bon or plus bien.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: To say where something is, use est or sont + a place word: Les clés sont sur la table. Many place words end in de: à côté de, près de, loin de. De + le becomes du: à côté du lit. Ici, là and là-bas say how far away something is.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Say how often with toujours, souvent, parfois, rarement and ne … jamais. They go right after the conjugated verb: Je vais souvent au marché. In the passé composé they sit between avoir/être and the participle: J'ai souvent travaillé.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. French always needs the pronoun before the verb: Je parle français. Use tu for a friend and vous for a stranger or several people; on means “we” in speech.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: Quelqu'un is someone and quelque chose is something. Their negatives are ne … personne and ne … rien: Je ne vois personne. Je n'ai rien. Use tout, chaque and autre for "all", "each" and "other": tous les jours, chaque matin, un autre café.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: Quelle heure est-il ? Il est huit heures. At what time? À huit heures. A day with no article is one day (lundi, this Monday). With le it is a habit (le lundi, every Monday).
grammatik.futur.intro: Use the futur simple for predictions, promises and plans: Demain, il pleuvra. Je vous appellerai ce soir. Take the infinitive (without the final -e of -re verbs) and add -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Common verbs have a special stem: je serai, j'aurai, j'irai, je ferai, je pourrai.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: A time clause tells when something happens: Quand il pleut, je prends le bus. Dès que j'aurai mon permis, j'achèterai une voiture. When the main clause is in the future, French also puts quand and dès que in the future, unlike English. Use avant de + infinitive when both verbs have the same subject: Avant de partir, j'appelle la banque.
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: Y replaces à + a thing or a place: Tu vas à la préfecture ? Oui, j'y vais. En replaces de + a thing, and it stands for quantities: Tu as besoin de ce formulaire ? Oui, j'en ai besoin. J'en veux deux. Il y en a trois. Both go before the verb.
grammatik.lassen.intro: Use faire + infinitive when someone else does the job for you or because of you: Je fais réparer ma voiture. Elle se fait couper les cheveux. Use laisser + infinitive to let something happen: Laissez-moi passer. Pronouns go before faire or laisser: Je la fais réparer.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Spoken French is full of small markers that start, close, hesitate or correct: bon, ben, enfin, quoi, du coup, voilà, bref, alors, en fait. Du coup, je suis venu à pied means "so, I walked". Enfin corrects yourself, bref sums up, en fait means "actually". Use them in speech and informal messages, not in a formal email. There, write donc or par conséquent instead of du coup.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives need a fixed preposition: content de, fier de, capable de, satisfait de, prêt à, habitué à, intéressé par, bon en, gentil avec. Il est content du résultat. Elle est habituée au bruit. After the preposition comes a noun or an infinitive: Je suis prêt à partir. If the subject changes, use que + subjunctive for feelings: Je suis content que tu viennes. Also learn facile à vs il est facile de.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: Linkers show how two ideas connect. Contrast: pourtant (yet), cependant (however), en revanche (on the other hand). Result: donc, alors, ainsi, c'est pourquoi. Explanation and addition: en effet, de plus, d'ailleurs. Most start a new sentence and are followed by a comma: Le loyer est cher. De plus, il y a des charges.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: To say what something is for, use pour + infinitive when the person is the same: Je travaille pour gagner ma vie. Use pour que + subjunctive when the person changes: Je répète pour que vous compreniez. In formal writing, afin de and afin que do the same job.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: When two pronouns stand before the verb, they follow a fixed order: Je le lui donne. Il me l'a dit. Je vous en parle. Il y en a trois. Me, te, se, nous, vous come first, then le, la, les, then lui, leur, then y, then en.
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: After a preposition, a thing needs lequel, laquelle, lesquels or lesquelles: le bureau dans lequel je travaille. For people, qui is enough: la personne avec qui j'ai parlé. À and de merge with lequel (auquel, duquel), and duquel follows compound prepositions such as à côté de. A relative clause takes the subjunctive when the thing is wanted but not known to exist, or after a superlative: Je cherche un appartement qui soit proche du métro.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: The subjonctif passé is avoir or être in the subjunctive plus the past participle: que tu sois venu, qu'elle ait fini. Use it for something finished before the main verb: Je suis content que tu sois venu hier. The subjonctif présent covers the same time or later: Je suis content que tu viennes demain. In modern French the tense of the main verb does not change this: Je voulais qu'il vienne.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: Devoir and pouvoir change their meaning with the tense. Il doit être malade means "he must be ill"; Il devait venir means "he was supposed to come"; Il aurait dû venir means "he should have come"; Il aurait pu venir means "he could have come". Il se peut que + subjunctive expresses possibility. In the news, the conditional marks unconfirmed information: Selon la police, le suspect serait en fuite. L'incendie aurait fait trois blessés.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: You can set a condition without si. After à condition que, pourvu que and à moins que the verb is in the subjunctive: Je signe à condition que le contrat soit clair. Au cas où takes the conditionnel, never the subjunctive: Au cas où tu serais en retard, appelle-moi. With the same subject, use à condition de or à moins de + infinitive. En cas de + noun and sauf si + indicative are the short forms.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: Formal writing shortens a clause into a participle: Ayant terminé son stage, Inès a été embauchée. The participle can carry its own subject (La réunion terminée, chacun est rentré) or stand alone (Arrivée à la préfecture, elle a pris un ticket). A participle alone must share the subject of the main clause, or you get the classic error ✗ Étant malade, mon patron m'a donné un jour. Étant donné and compte tenu de are fixed forms. In speech, use quand, comme or après avoir.
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: Formal French packs a whole clause into a noun group: Les loyers ont augmenté becomes la hausse des loyers. Letters, emails from HR and headlines use this all the time. Learn each noun with its gender: la fermeture, le report, le départ. In speech the verbs stay, and too many nouns make a text heavy.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Letters from the préfecture, memos and reports link ideas with formal words. What comes next decides which one you can use: a noun (en raison de, compte tenu de), a clause (étant donné que, dans la mesure où) or a new sentence (néanmoins, par conséquent). Careful: Or at the start of a sentence is not the word for “or”.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: Comme si compares something with a situation that is not real: Il parle comme s'il savait tout. After comme si use the imparfait for the same time and the plus-que-parfait for an earlier time: Il agit comme si rien ne s'était passé. Fixed phrases: faire comme si, comme si de rien n'était. Quand bien même + conditionnel means "even if" in formal French: Quand bien même il aurait raison, il devrait s'excuser. Même si + indicative is the everyday version.
grammatik.futur-2.intro: The futur antérieur (avoir or être in the futur + participe passé) shows that something will be finished before another future action or moment: D'ici vendredi, j'aurai fini. Quand tu arriveras, nous aurons dîné. After quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, une fois que and après que it marks the first of two future actions, where English uses the present perfect: Dès que j'aurai reçu le récépissé, je vous l'enverrai. It is also used to guess about the past: Il aura oublié son rendez-vous.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: A cleft sentence puts one element in the spotlight: C'est Léa qui a signé le bail (the subject, with qui) or C'est demain que j'ai rendez-vous (anything else, with que), also C'est à la préfecture que Mamadou a rendez-vous. The verb agrees with the pronoun before qui: C'est moi qui suis responsable. Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le délai and Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'une attestation split the sentence in two. In speech, dislocation does a similar job: Mon dossier, je l'ai déposé hier.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A formal text holds together through links, not through repetition. To point back to the last-named person or thing, use celui-ci or ce dernier: Karim a vu le directeur ; ce dernier a approuvé le projet. A noun with ce / cette sums up the previous sentence: Les loyers ont augmenté. Cette hausse touche les jeunes. Order your points with d'abord, ensuite, enfin or d'une part … d'autre part, and add one with en outre. In writing cela replaces the spoken ça, and ledit / ladite appear in legal texts (recognition only).
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: The passé simple is a past tense of books, not of conversation, and you only need to recognise it: Il parla, puis il partit. You meet it in novels, tales, biographies and history books, mostly in the 3rd person (il fut, il eut, ils partirent). In speech and everyday writing the passé composé replaces it: Il a parlé, puis il est parti. Watch the traps: il finit and il dit can be present or passé simple, il vit is vivre or voir, and il fut is not il fit.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Some French verbs look alike for an English speaker but are not interchangeable. Je sais nager, but je connais Karim. Nous visitons un musée, but nous rendons visite à nos voisins. Amener, apporter, emmener and emporter depend on people or things, and on the direction.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: After il faut que, je veux que, j'aimerais que and verbs of feeling (je suis content que, j'ai peur que) the verb after que is in the subjunctive: Il faut que tu viennes. Je suis content que tu sois là. But after espérer, penser, croire and savoir you use the indicative: J'espère que tu viendras. Je pense qu'il a raison.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: French uses le, la, les for things in general and for known things: J'aime le café. Un, une, des is for one or a new thing: Il y a une pharmacie. There is no article for jobs after être (Elle est infirmière), after parler (Je parle français), after beaucoup de and pas de.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: This or that: ce livre, cette maison, ces livres. Before a masculine word that starts with a vowel or a mute h, use cet: cet hôtel. French has no separate “near” and “far” word: ce means this and that, and you add -ci or -là to choose. Quel, quelle, quels, quelles mean which or what.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.brief:
Why “J'aime le café” but “Je parle français”? Why “Elle est infirmière” with no article?

  • —No article: jobs and nationalities after être, languages after parler, after beaucoup de, pas de, sans.
  • un, une, desOne of many, or a new thing: il y a une pharmacie. (du, de la = some.)
  • le, la, lesThe one we both know, and things in general with aimer: j'aime le café.

kultur.sourcingNote:
Every topic here is factual knowledge: publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in France (laws, who is responsible, what you do), written by icanspeak French with reference to official sources such as service-public.fr, vie-publique.fr, ameli.fr and the ministries. France comes first; the topics on the francophone world follow.
What is deliberately NOT here: claims about “the French character”. Nothing is claimed about people; rules, figures and responsibilities are, and where practice differs by region, commune or person, the topic says so.
Rules and figures change. A figure carries its date; if in doubt, the official source is right, not this page. This is general orientation, not legal advice.

akk.regel.intro: The direct object (COD) is the person or thing the verb acts on, with no preposition: Je vois Ana. Je cherche mes clés. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: Je la vois. Before a vowel or a mute h, me, te, le, la become m', t', l': Je l'aime.
akk.regel.example: Common mistake: Je vois la. → Je la vois. With an infinitive, the pronoun goes before the infinitive: Je vais la voir. In the negative it stays next to its verb: Je ne la vois pas. In the passé composé it goes before avoir, and the participle agrees: Je l'ai vue. Don't mix it up with lui, leur (à + a person): Je lui parle.

sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.1: Full sentences, not a list: “J'ai 29 ans.”, not just “29”. Age goes with avoir, and a job takes no article: “Je suis électricien.”
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.2: End with your free time: it is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.3: You say je; the examiner says vous to you (“Comment vous appelez-vous ?”), so listen for the vous form.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.0: “Sur la photo, je vois …” is the easiest way to start. Learn each noun with its article: une gare, un quai, un train.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.1: “Je pense que …” and “peut-être que …” let you guess without being sure.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.2: The last sentence is about you: that is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.0: First count (“il y a deux personnes”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.1: For what is happening now, use the present or être en train de + infinitive: il cuisine, il est en train de cuisiner.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.0: French needs a small word before food: des fruits, des légumes, du pain, de la viande. You cannot say “j'achète fruits”.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.1: “à la caisse”, “par carte”, “en espèces”: learn the little word with the phrase.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.2: A time phrase at the end (“le samedi”, “une fois par semaine”) sounds practised straight away.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.0: Two people, two descriptions: first the boy, then the girl.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.1: One sentence about the weather, with “il fait”: il fait beau, il fait chaud, il fait froid.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.2: “parce que” joins your reason to your sentence: j'aime le parc parce que c'est calme.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Say what is au premier plan and à l'arrière-plan: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “Je pense que c'est …, parce que …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 a comparison like this is a natural last step.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: Say how someone feels and why: “Elle a l'air inquiète. Peut-être que …” Pictures with people often invite this question.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.1: Say what you can and can't see: “On ne voit que son bras.”
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A real detail from your own life (“parfois, j'attends une semaine”) is worth more than a general sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-bewerbungsgesprae: Use place words to organise what you say: à gauche, à droite, en face de, au fond.
Show that a guess is a guess (“Je dirais que …”, “il se peut qu'elle soit …”) and give a reason.
The part in the past is expected at B1: the passé composé for the event (“j'ai passé”), the imparfait for how you felt (“j'avais peur”).
One sentence with “À mon avis”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part. In a real interview the recruiter and you would use vous.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: “Je suppose que …, parce que …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a word (alternance) instead of just saying it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The “pourquoi ?” question gets a real answer with “parce que” or “Une raison pourrait être que …”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: Show how you know something: “On voit que …, parce que …”
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: “Maintenant …” shows how things have changed, which is a useful B1 skill. At an official's desk you say vous.
You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with the conditional: je proposerais, je choisirais, on pourrait … ?
Register: tu, because you are colleagues in the same team. With a manager or a stranger you would switch to vous.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: un avantage évident, en revanche, il ne faut pas oublier.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: Saying “pas seulement …, mais aussi …” shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: Something you notice in the picture supports your argument (“Ce qui me frappe, c'est que …”), not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own view is there (“Certains diront que …”) and you answer it.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between “des jours de présence pour toute l'équipe” and “une règle pour chaque personne” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“La vraie question n'est pas de savoir si …, mais comment …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: “Recycler limite les dégâts ; cela ne règle pas le problème”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.

ac.find.r: “{word}” has r: say it at the back of the mouth, with friction, and keep the tip of your tongue down. Not the English r, not a roll.
ac.find.uou: “{word}”: u is “ee” with round lips (tongue forward), ou is “oo” with the tongue back. tu is not tout.
ac.find.nasal: “{word}”: the vowel is nasal. Let the air go through your nose, and don't say a closing n or “g”.
ac.find.eu: “{word}” has eu: say é and round your lips. It is not ou (deux ≠ doux).
ac.find.emuet: In “{word}” the e is silent or weak. Don't give it a full vowel: table sounds like “tabl”.
ac.find.liaison: “{word}” follows a word that links to it: the last letter before it is said (s as z, n as n), and it joins the vowel.
ac.find.enchainement: “{word}” follows straight on from the word before. No small stop in your throat: the consonant before it slides on to the vowel.
ac.find.silent: In “{word}” the last letter is silent. Don't say it.
ac.find.sz: “{word}”: s between two vowels is z, a double ss is s, and ç is s. Keep your voice on for z.
ac.find.chj: “{word}”: ch is sh as in “shop”, and j (or g before e, i) is the voiced sound in “measure”. Not “dj”, not a rasp.
ac.find.bv: “{word}”: b uses both lips, v uses your top teeth on your bottom lip, with voice. vin is not bain.
ac.find.aspiration: “{word}” has p, t or k. Say it with no puff of air.
ac.find.stress: “{word}”: keep the syllables even. Don't push a syllable inside the word; the end of the group is a little longer.
ac.find.double: “{word}” has a double letter. Say one short consonant, don't hold it.
ac.find.voiced: In “{word}” keep your voice on until the end of the last consonant. It must not turn into p, t, k or s.
ac.find.pb: “{word}” has p or b: p has no voice and no puff of air; for b your voice is on from the start.
ac.find.vowels: “{word}”: keep every vowel pure and full. No glide (é is not “ay”), no weak “uh”.
ac.find.h: The h in “{word}” is silent. Start straight on the next vowel.

mhelp.aria: Help: what is this page for?
mhelp.kultur.what: Here you learn how everyday life in France works: meal times, proving your address, the médecin traitant, public holidays and much more.
mhelp.kultur.s1: Pick a topic at your level (A1, A2 …).
mhelp.kultur.s2: Read the short text and look at the examples.
mhelp.kultur.s3: Then answer the quiz questions. That way you remember what matters.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.what: Etymology is the story of a word: where it comes from, how it used to sound and what it used to mean. Most French words come from Latin, many from Frankish (the Germanic language of the Franks), and others from Arabic, English, Italian and more, so some may be related to words in your language.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s1: “The root” shows the oldest form of the word we know.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s2: Read the family tree from the bottom up: from the root to the words of today.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s3: “Tracing it in other languages” shows the word in your language. Tip: tap the speaker to hear the word.
mhelp.grammatik.what: Every grammar topic, sorted by level — each with a rule and exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s1: Choose your level and a topic, or follow the guided path to go step by step in the right order.
mhelp.grammatik.s2: Read the rule first, then do the exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s3: Your results are saved. You can see them under „Mein Fortschritt“.
mhelp.hoeren.what: Practise listening: announcements, phone calls, conversations and radio pieces from A1 to B2.
mhelp.hoeren.s1: Choose a text at your level.
mhelp.hoeren.s2: Listen as often as you like — slower, too.
mhelp.hoeren.s3: Answer the questions. Afterwards the transcript helps you.
mhelp.lesen.what: Practise reading with real kinds of text: signs, adverts, emails and articles.
mhelp.lesen.s1: Choose a task at your level.
mhelp.lesen.s2: Read the text calmly. There is no rush.
mhelp.lesen.s3: Answer the questions and read the explanation for each answer.
mhelp.sprechen.what: Practise speaking as in the exam: describe pictures, introduce yourself, plan together, discuss.
mhelp.sprechen.s2: Start the timer and speak out loud. The useful phrases help you.
mhelp.sprechen.s3: Afterwards, compare with the model answer.

nsw.why.title: Why look things up?
nsw.why.p1: Nobody learns every form by heart – native speakers look things up too. If you know where the answer is, you write with more confidence and don't have to guess.
nsw.why.p2: And the best part: every time you look something up, it sticks a little better. You learn along the way.

nsw.what.title: What is a reference?
nsw.what.p: You don't read a reference from cover to cover. You open it when you have a question – and find the answer in seconds: as a table, with a rule and an example sentence.

nsw.ueben.p: You learn a topic step by step: rule, exercises, feedback.
nsw.nach.title: Look it up
nsw.nach.p: You have a specific question – during homework, in an email, just before the exam. Look it up, keep writing.
nsw.tips.title: How it helps you
nsw.tip1.p: Not sure about a form? Look it up instead of guessing.
nsw.tip2.p: A word like “fui” or “roto”? The verb tables give you the base form.
nsw.tip3.p: Irregular verbs and verbs with prepositions come up in many exams. Going through the lists once is worth it.
nsw.tip4.p: Every page can be printed, shared and played as a live quiz with the whole class.

sprachen.legend.region: Official, beside other languages at home
sprachen.benrath.text: French grew out of the Latin spoken in northern Gaul and became the language of the French state. From the 16th century it travelled with explorers, settlers and colonial rule to North America, the Caribbean, Africa, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. Today most French speakers live outside France, and more than half of those who use it every day live in Africa.

sprachen.c.FRA: Where French began, and the variety this course teaches. French is the language of the Republic (Article 2 of the Constitution); regional languages such as Breton, Occitan and Alsatian are recognised as part of France's heritage. Overseas France, from the Antilles to Réunion and New Caledonia, speaks French too.
sprachen.c.MCO: French is the official language of the principality. Monégasque, a local Ligurian language, is taught at school, and Italian is widely heard.
sprachen.c.BEL: French is one of three official languages, beside Dutch and German. It is the language of Wallonia and of most people in Brussels; Flanders speaks Dutch. Belgians say septante and nonante for 70 and 90.
sprachen.c.CHE: French is one of four national languages, spoken in the west (la Suisse romande): Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura and parts of Fribourg, the Valais and Bern. Many Swiss say septante, huitante, nonante.
sprachen.c.LUX: Luxembourg has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, French and German. French is the language of the law and of much of working life, and many cross-border workers from France use it every day.
sprachen.c.CAN: French and English are Canada's two official languages. Most French speakers live in Québec, where French is the only official language of the province; New Brunswick is officially bilingual, and Acadians and Franco-Ontarians keep their own communities. If you are heading for Canada, get used to Québec French early.
sprachen.c.HTI: French and Haitian Creole are both official. Almost everyone speaks Creole at home; French is used at school, in the law and in formal writing.
sprachen.c.SEN: French is the official language, and Wolof is the language most people use in daily life. Senegalese French borrows from Wolof and has words of its own.
sprachen.c.CIV: French is the official language and, in Abidjan, often the first language of young people. Ivorian French and the street slang nouchi are heard in music across the French-speaking world.
sprachen.c.GIN: French is the official language, beside national languages such as Pular, Maninka and Susu.
sprachen.c.BEN: French is the official language. Fon and Yoruba are among the languages most widely spoken at home.
sprachen.c.TGO: French is the official language; Ewe and Kabiyè are national languages that many people speak at home.
sprachen.c.CMR: Cameroon has two official languages, French and English, from its French and British past. Most regions are French-speaking; the North-West and South-West are English-speaking.
sprachen.c.TCD: French and Arabic are both official. Chadian Arabic is the common language of the street in much of the country.
sprachen.c.CAF: French and Sango are both official. Sango is the language almost everyone shares.
sprachen.c.GAB: French is the official language and, in the cities, many people's first language. Fang is the largest of the national languages.
sprachen.c.COG: French is the official language. Lingala and Kituba are the national languages of everyday life.
sprachen.c.COD: One of the largest French-speaking countries in the world by population. French is official, beside four national languages: Lingala, Swahili, Kikongo and Tshiluba.
sprachen.c.GNQ: Spanish, French and Portuguese are all official. French was added in the late 1990s; the country's neighbours are French-speaking.
sprachen.c.RWA: French is official beside Kinyarwanda, English and Swahili. Schools switched from French to English in 2008, but many adults still speak French.
sprachen.c.BDI: Kirundi, French and English are official. Kirundi is the language of nearly everyone; French is used in government and education.
sprachen.c.DJI: French and Arabic are the official languages; Somali and Afar are the languages most people speak at home.
sprachen.c.MDG: Malagasy and French are both official. Malagasy is everyone's language; French is used in education, business and the press.
sprachen.c.COM: Comorian (Shikomori), Arabic and French are official. Mayotte, a French département, belongs to the same island group.
sprachen.c.SYC: Seychellois Creole, English and French are all official. The Creole is French-based, so many words sound familiar.
sprachen.c.VUT: Bislama, English and French are official. Schools teach either in English or in French.
sprachen.c.MUS: English is the language of parliament, but French is the language of the press and much of business, and Mauritian Creole, which is French-based, is almost everyone's home language.
sprachen.c.MLI: The 2023 constitution made Mali's national languages official and kept French as a working language. French is still used widely in government, schools and business.
sprachen.c.BFA: A constitutional change in 2023 made the national languages official and French a working language. French is still used in administration, education and the media.
sprachen.c.NER: Recent reforms have given the national languages, above all Hausa, a stronger status, and French is now a working language. It is still common in administration, schools and the media.
sprachen.c.MRT: Arabic is the only official language, but French is still widely used in business, higher education and the press.
sprachen.c.MAR: Arabic and Tamazight are the official languages, but French is the language of much of business, banking, science and higher education. Many Moroccans switch between Darija and French.
sprachen.c.DZA: Arabic and Tamazight are official, and Algeria is not a member of the Francophonie, yet it is one of the countries with the most French speakers. French is everywhere in the press, business and higher education.
sprachen.c.TUN: Arabic is the official language. French is widely used in business, medicine, higher education and the media, and many signs are in both.
sprachen.c.LBN: Arabic is the official language. French is taught at many schools and used in law and business, and many Lebanese switch between Arabic, French and English.
sprachen.m.louisiane: French came to Louisiana with French settlers and with the Acadians expelled from Canada in the 18th century, whose descendants are the Cajuns. Few young people speak Louisiana French at home today, but many schools teach it in immersion classes.
sprachen.m.aoste: An Italian region where French is official beside Italian. Many local people also speak Franco-Provençal (the patois valdôtain).
sprachen.m.pondichery: A French trading post in India until 1954. A small community still speaks French, and French street names and a French lycée remain.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: French is a Romance language: it grew out of the Latin spoken in Roman Gaul, with words from the Gaulish Celts before it and the Germanic Franks after it. Romance belongs to the large Indo-European family, so many languages from Iceland to India share distant roots with French.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to French, though many have lived beside it for a long time, in Africa, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. That doesn't make French harder: it just means you learn words fresh rather than recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in English. The tree is simplified: exactly where Catalan and Franco-Provençal belong is debated.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.englisch: English is Germanic, but after 1066 it took thousands of words from Norman French, so you can already read a lot of French: hôpital, animal, possible, important. The word decoder below shows the patterns. The new parts are gender (le, la), verb endings, nasal vowels and the many silent letters.
sprachen.cmp.deutsch: German is Germanic, a distant relative of French: Mutter – mère, drei – trois. You already know grammatical gender and verb endings, which helps. French has only two genders and no cases on nouns, but nasal vowels are new, and the gender often differs from German: le soleil, la lune.
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: Spanish is a close relative: most grammar will feel familiar, from gender and articles to the subjunctive and two past tenses. The hard parts are the sounds (nasal vowels, the French u, silent endings) and the subject: French always needs it, so it is je parle, never just parle.
sprachen.cmp.portugiesisch: Portuguese is a close relative and shares French's nasal vowels, so your ear has a head start. Grammar is familiar: gender, the subjunctive, two past tenses. Watch the gender of some nouns: a árvore but l'arbre (m.), o mar but la mer.
sprachen.cmp.italienisch: Italian is a close relative, with similar verbs, articles and two past tenses. French spelling is the big change: many final letters are silent (ils parlent), and nasal vowels are new. Watch false friends: salire means to go up, but French salir means to make dirty.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to French. But the two have lived side by side for a long time, and French has taken words from Arabic: café, sucre, magasin, algèbre, toubib (doctor, informal). French is written left to right with every vowel, and it has p and v, which Arabic does not.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary. For grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: English → French: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: After 1066 English took thousands of words from French, and many more from Latin. So many long English words are French words in disguise. If you know English, these patterns let you guess, and often say, hundreds of French words.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a pattern: English on the left, French on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: English word → French word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a word you know: swap the pattern and say it the French way. Often you get a real French word, and people will understand you.
sprachen.dec.note: They're rules of thumb: not every word fits, and accents and gender have to be learned (almost every -té word is feminine: la qualité). Watch out for false friends: actuellement means currently, une librairie is a bookshop, sensible means sensitive, and une location is a rental.
sprachen.dec.quiz: Try it yourself: what is it in French?

dialekte.title: Accents of French in France
dialekte.lead: From Lille to Marseille: how French sounds in different parts of France, which regional languages you will meet there, and how French differs in Québec, Belgium, Switzerland and Africa. Pick a region for examples and typical features.
dialekte.map.title: The accent map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show five big groups: the north, the centre and east, the Midi (the south), Corsica, and the regions with a second language. The dots are well-known city accents and France's regional languages.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several words, and people move around. Pain au chocolat and serpillière are understood everywhere.
dialekte.group.oil.text: The langue d'oïl area, where standard French grew up. The e in petite falls away, nasal vowels are pure, and many people say brin and brun the same way. This is the pronunciation this course teaches.
dialekte.group.transition.text: Auvergne and Limousin lie just south of the old oïl/oc line, Lyon and the Alps in the Franco-Provençal area. The accent sits between north and south: close to the standard, with local words and a melody of its own.
dialekte.group.midi.text: The south, where Occitan was spoken: every e is sounded (pe-ti-te), nasal vowels end in a light ng (pain sounds like «peng»), and the o of rose is open. Warm, sing-song and easy to recognise.
dialekte.group.corse.text: French with the rhythm of Corsican, a language close to Italian: clear vowels, a rolled r for some speakers, and Corsican place names on every sign.
dialekte.group.bilingue.text: French here is close to the standard, with a melody, some sounds and some words from Breton, Alsatian, Basque or Catalan.
dialekte.r.paris: The French of the national media and of most textbooks, though the rest of France hears Parisians as fast and a little clipped. Casual speech drops a lot: the ne of negatives and the e of je (je ne sais pas → chais pas). Slang and verlan travel from the suburbs into everyday speech.
dialekte.r.nord: Close to the standard in the cities. Traditional speech (ch'ti, from Picard) has ch where French has c or s: ch'est for c'est. Some local words are shared with Belgium, such as drache for a downpour. A film made ch'ti famous across France in 2008.
dialekte.r.ouest: The west of the langue d'oïl area, close to the standard. People in Tours are often told they speak the 'purest' French: a myth, but the accent is easy for learners. Normandy is known for its careful non-answers, and the west calls a plastic bag une poche.
dialekte.r.est: Lorraine, Champagne, Burgundy and Franche-Comté. Close to the standard, with a slightly drawn-out melody in Lorraine, where some people sound the t of vingt. In rural Burgundy some older people still roll their r.
dialekte.r.centre: South of the old oïl/oc line, where Occitan dialects were spoken. The accent is milder than in the Midi, but many people sound the e. Families from Auvergne once ran many of the cafés of Paris.
dialekte.r.lyon: The Franco-Provençal area, between oïl and oc. Lyon speech is close to the standard, with words of its own (gone, mâchon) and some shared with Switzerland and Savoy, such as panosse.
dialekte.r.sudouest: An accent many French people find the warmest: every e sounded, nasal vowels with ng, and a clear rhythm. The south-west defends chocolatine against pain au chocolat. Gascon and Occitan words colour everyday speech.
dialekte.r.provence: The famous accent du Midi, known from films and songs. Every syllable is sounded, so French has a different rhythm here: une petite maison sounds like «une petiteu maisong». Words from Provençal are everywhere: fada, peuchère, pitchoun.
dialekte.r.corse: French is the everyday language, but Corsican (corsu), close to Tuscan Italian, is taught at school and appears on bilingual signs: Aiacciu, Bastia, Portivechju. The French spoken here takes its rhythm and some words from it.
dialekte.r.bretagne: French is the language of daily life. Breton, a Celtic language related to Welsh, was spoken in the west, and Gallo, a langue d'oïl, in the east. Both are taught in some schools, and road signs are often bilingual: Kemper for Quimper, Roazhon for Rennes.
dialekte.r.alsace: Many older people grew up with Alsatian, a Germanic dialect close to the German of Baden and Switzerland. Alsatian French has a firm, clear sound and some German habits, such as ou bien at the end of a question. Alsace and Moselle also keep some local rules, including two extra public holidays.
dialekte.r.paysbasque: In the French Basque Country (Iparralde), Basque (euskara) is spoken beside French, taught in many schools and written on signs. Béarn, to the east, is Gascon country. The French of the whole area has the southern sounded e and ng.
dialekte.r.roussillon: The Pyrénées-Orientales, which locals also call Northern Catalonia. Catalan is spoken by a minority, taught at school and seen on signs (Perpinyà for Perpignan). The French has a southern accent with a Catalan colour.
dialekte.m.marseille: The best-known southern accent: loud, quick and full of humour. Marseille speech mixes Provençal, Italian and Arabic words into French. You don't need to copy it, but expect to hear it in films, songs and on the radio.
dialekte.m.toulouse: The ville rose speaks with a warm south-western accent: every e sounded and nasal vowels ending in ng. Adieu as a greeting surprises many visitors, and asking for a pain au chocolat starts a friendly argument.
dialekte.m.lille: City French is close to the standard. In the Nord you still hear ch'ti words in families, in songs and at the market, and many are shared with Belgium across the border.
dialekte.m.brezhoneg: A Celtic language, related to Welsh and Cornish, not to French. Breton is taught in Diwan schools and bilingual classes, but like every regional language of France it has no official status, and most fluent speakers are older.
dialekte.m.occitan: The langue d'oc of the south, with dialects such as Provençal, Languedocien, Gascon, Limousin and Auvergnat. It gave French many words and shaped the southern accent. Few people speak it daily now, but it is taught, sung and heard in the Toulouse metro.
dialekte.m.alsacien: A group of Alemannic and Frankish German dialects. Part of the population still speaks Alsatian, mostly older people, and schools teach it beside standard German.
dialekte.m.corsu: An Italo-Romance language close to Tuscan. Corsican is taught at school and at the University of Corsica, and it lives on in songs, above all the polyphonic singing the island is known for.
dialekte.m.euskara: Basque is not related to French or to any other known language. In France it is spoken in Labourd, Lower Navarre and Soule; schools called ikastola teach in Basque.
dialekte.m.catala: Spoken in Roussillon, the north of historic Catalonia, which became French in 1659. It is the same language as in Barcelona, with a local colour.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines across France
dialekte.lines.lead: Two old language borders still explain much of what you hear. The lines on the map show roughly where they ran; real borders are wide and blurred, and they mark where the old languages were spoken, not where French changes overnight.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: The oïl/oc line: oïl | oc
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: In the Middle Ages the north said oïl for yes (it became oui) and the south said oc. North of the line grew the langues d'oïl, from which standard French came; south of it, Occitan. The southern accent of French (sounded e, ng after nasal vowels) roughly follows the old oc area. Around Lyon and in the Alps lies a third area, Franco-Provençal.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: The Breton line: Breton | Gallo
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: West of the line people traditionally spoke Breton, a Celtic language; east of it, Gallo, a langue d'oïl close to French. The line on the map is the one recorded in the late 19th century, from Plouha to the Gulf of Morbihan; over the centuries it had moved west. Today almost everyone in Brittany speaks French first.
dialekte.lines.note: Simplified: inside every group there are many local accents, and the same person may speak differently at work and at home. Spelling never changes: everyone writes petite, pain and rose.
dialekte.world.title: French outside France
dialekte.world.lead: This course teaches the standard French of France, but your colleagues, neighbours and favourite series may not use it. All these varieties understand each other and share one spelling. The biggest differences: the numbers in Belgium and Switzerland, the meal names in Québec and Switzerland, and the sounds and words of Québec.
dialekte.w.quebec: Almost nine million people live in Québec, most of them French speakers: the largest French-speaking community in the Americas. Québec French has its own sounds (t and d before i and u sound like ts and dz: «tsu»), its own words (char, magasiner) and English loanwords in casual speech, while official usage replaces English words firmly (courriel for e-mail). If you are heading for Canada, listen to it early.
dialekte.w.acadie: The French of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, in some ways older than Québec French: je parlons for nous parlons, and old words such as asteure. In south-east New Brunswick, chiac mixes French and English freely.
dialekte.w.belgique: French is one of three official languages, spoken in Wallonia and Brussels. The accent is close to that of the Nord, and two numbers are easier: septante (70) and nonante (90). For 80, Belgians say quatre-vingts, as in France.
dialekte.w.suisse: French is spoken in the west, la Suisse romande: Geneva, Lausanne, Neuchâtel, Fribourg, the Valais. The pace is calmer, the numbers are septante and nonante, and in some cantons huitante. Meals are déjeuner, dîner and souper, as in Québec.
dialekte.w.afriqueouest: French is official or widely used in more than twenty African countries, mostly beside African languages people speak at home. Each country has its own words and expressions; Abidjan and Dakar set trends, and their music and slang travel to France.
dialekte.w.maghreb: In Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia French is not official, but it is widely used in business, higher education and the media, beside Arabic and Tamazight. Many people switch between Darija and French in one sentence, and you hear this mix in France too.
dialekte.w.antilles: In Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion and Mayotte, French is the official language, and Creoles (in Mayotte, Shimaore) are spoken every day. These are French départements, so the rules, schools and documents are the same as in mainland France.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn an accent?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Use the standard French you learn here: it is understood everywhere and works in every exam, préfecture and workplace. Do listen to other accents, though: your neighbours, colleagues and the radio use them, and listening tests in French exams may include voices from Belgium, Switzerland, Québec or Africa. There is no need to copy an accent; just get used to hearing it.
dialekte.src.title: Sources
dialekte.src.text: A simplified overview following the usual descriptions of regional French and of the languages of France, such as those of the Délégation générale à la langue française et aux langues de France (culture.gouv.fr). The word maps for pain au chocolat and the floor cloth simplify published surveys of regional French. Map outlines: Natural Earth (public domain); the inner borders are drawn by hand and rough.

satzmelodie.lead: Same words, a different melody: at the end of the sentence your voice goes down ↘ or up ↗. Listen, compare and repeat.
satzmelodie.note.none: No recordings yet — your browser reads the sentences aloud.
satzmelodie.note.some: {n} of {total} sentences have a recording. Your browser reads the others aloud.
satzmelodie.task1.title: Listen and compare the melody.
satzmelodie.task1.text: Repeat after me: after each sentence you have time to say it out loud. With the microphone 🎤 next to a sentence you can check your own melody – the recording stays on your device.
satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: in French, “Léa arrive demain?” and “Léa arrive demain.” have the same words, so the melody is what makes it a question. A normal yes/no question rises a little. An echo question rises much higher, and it means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right (“Quoi, elle arrive demain?”).
satzmelodie.mic.title: Repeat and check
satzmelodie.task2.title: Listen. Statement, question or exclamation?
satzmelodie.task2.text: The words are always the same. Only the melody is different. Add the punctuation marks.
satzmelodie.task3.title: Which word is stressed? Click it.
satzmelodie.task3.text: The answer is always the same sentence. The question decides which word gets the stress.
satzmelodie.task4.title: Melody maze: which exit?
satzmelodie.task4.text: Quaki hops through the sentence with the voice. At the end the path splits: does the voice go up, down, or steeply down? Then you see the real melody – and Quaki rides along it.
satzmelodie.lab.aria: Maze: at the end of the sentence the path splits into three exits – top: question, bottom: statement, very bottom: exclamation.
satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end. The last syllable of the group is a little higher and longer before it falls.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice usually falls at the end, as in a statement. Questions with qui, que, quand, où, comment, combien, pourquoi, quel. With a gentle rise instead, they sound extra friendly.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: Often the same words as a statement: only the melody makes it a question (Vous venez du Portugal?). The voice rises at the end. With est-ce que or inversion it rises too.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: The voice rises high at the end. You're surprised or checking what you heard. French often starts it with Quoi or Comment, or just repeats the words.
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes very high, then the voice falls a long way. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: On each item the voice rises a little → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.
satzmelodie.teacherTip: For teachers: a pair activity with three cards (. ? !). A says “Léa arrive demain” with one melody, B holds up the matching card.
satzmelodie.res.noRecorder: Your browser can't record here. Try Chrome, Edge or Safari.
satzmelodie.res.noMic: It doesn't work without a microphone: allow access in the address bar and tap the microphone again.
satzmelodie.res.speak: Speak now: “{text}” – tap the microphone when you're done.
satzmelodie.res.tooQuiet: I hardly heard anything. Speak a bit louder and closer to the microphone.
satzmelodie.res.echoTip: In an echo question the voice goes up sharply at the end, even more clearly than in a yes/no question.
satzmelodie.res.endQuiet: The end of the sentence was too quiet to judge.
satzmelodie.res.noModel: There's no recording for this sentence yet – so only the end of the sentence is checked.
satzmelodie.res.failed: The recording couldn't be analysed. Try again.
satzmelodie.why.aussage: Statement: the voice goes down at the end ↘.
satzmelodie.why.echo: Echo question: the voice goes clearly up at the end ↗. You're surprised or checking that you heard right. A normal yes/no question rises much less.
satzmelodie.why.ausruf: Exclamation: the voice starts high and falls sharply ↘. You're excited or surprised.
satzmelodie.stress.ok: Correct! This word is the new information.
satzmelodie.stress.again: Try again: which word answers the question directly?
