wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to French.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the present tense are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: present, past and future, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the “beaten path”.
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: “Desirable difficulties”: what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.

wortfallen.lead: Some words look like a word you already know, or almost like a word in your own language, and mean something completely different. Here are {n} traps, each with a memory trick.
wortfallen.actuellement.react: Currently? So tomorrow you might like it?
wortfallen.actuellement.tip: False friend for English speakers (actually). For German (aktuell), Spanish (actualmente), Portuguese (atualmente) and Italian (attualmente) the word means the same as in French: at present. Actually is en fait or vraiment.
wortfallen.assister.m1: to attend, to be present at
wortfallen.assister.react: You wait for a French class every Tuesday? Does it never start?
wortfallen.assister.tip: False friend for English speakers (to attend = assister à), and for Spanish and Portuguese speakers (atender, to serve someone). French attendre means to wait.
wortfallen.esperer.react: Hoping for the bus? It has abandoned you.
wortfallen.esperer.tip: False friend for Spanish (esperar) and Portuguese (esperar), where the same word means both to wait and to hope. In French espérer is only to hope, and attendre is to wait. Italian: aspettare = attendre, sperare = espérer.
wortfallen.librairie.react: A shop where books are free? Good luck with the cashier.
wortfallen.librairie.tip: False friend for English speakers (library). Spanish librería, Portuguese livraria and Italian libreria also mean a bookshop. You borrow in a bibliothèque (or médiathèque in many towns) and buy in a librairie.
wortfallen.blesser.react: A priest who hurts the house? Call the police.
wortfallen.blesser.tip: False friend for English speakers (bless). Blesser means to injure: il est blessé = he is hurt. Bénir means to bless. Il a mal is for pain; je me suis blessé is the accident.
wortfallen.sensible.react: A sensitive boss who cries over his decisions? Hmm.
wortfallen.sensible.tip: False friend for English speakers (sensible = reasonable). For German (sensibel), Spanish (sensible) and Italian (sensibile) it is a true friend: sensitive.
wortfallen.monnaie.react: No change for the rent? The landlord wants a bank transfer.
wortfallen.monnaie.tip: False friend for English speakers (money). La monnaie is the coins you get back, small change, and also a currency (la monnaie européenne). Money in general is l'argent.
wortfallen.location.m1: a rental (of a flat, a car)
wortfallen.location.react: A rental of the meeting? Is there a deposit?
wortfallen.location.tip: False friend for English speakers (location). You will see location on every flat listing: it is a rental. A place is un lieu or un endroit, and the address is l'adresse.
wortfallen.chair.react: Sit on flesh? No, thank you.
wortfallen.chair.tip: False friend for English speakers (chair). A chair to sit on is une chaise, an armchair is un fauteuil. La chair is the flesh, as in la chair de poule (goosebumps).
wortfallen.preservatif.react: Condoms in the jam? That would not be a good recipe.
wortfallen.preservatif.tip: False friend for English speakers (preservative). Le préservatif is a condom. In a list of ingredients you will find conservateur, often with E200 to E299.
wortfallen.gymnase.react: She trains for the baccalauréat with weights?
wortfallen.gymnase.tip: False friend for German speakers (Gymnasium). A gymnase is a sports hall. The school for 15 to 18 year olds is the lycée (the collège comes before it).
wortfallen.recevoir.react: You turn into a present? Strange birthday.
wortfallen.recevoir.tip: False friend for German speakers (bekommen = to get). Devenir is to become. Receiving something is recevoir (and obtenir for a document, un titre de séjour).
wortfallen.constipe.react: Constipated through the nose? Then we need a different doctor.
wortfallen.constipe.tip: False friend for Spanish (constipado), Portuguese (constipado, in Portugal) and Italian (costipato) speakers: these words mean having a cold. French constipé is a problem with digestion. A cold is un rhume: je suis enrhumé, j'ai un rhume.
wortfallen.large.react: A wide film? Does the screen not fit?
wortfallen.large.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (largo = long). In French large is wide: une rue large. Long is long, for length and for time. Portuguese and Italian largo also mean wide.
wortfallen.salir.react: Make your friends dirty? Take a bath first.
wortfallen.salir.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (salir = to go out) and for Italian speakers (salire = to go up: monter in French). In French salir means to make dirty: salir ses vêtements. The adjective is sale.
wortfallen.enceinte.react: Embarrassed about a baby? No need to be.
wortfallen.enceinte.tip: False friend for Spanish speakers (embarazada = pregnant). French embarrassé means embarrassed, awkward. Pregnant is enceinte: say it as ma sœur est enceinte. Portuguese embaraçada and Italian imbarazzata mean embarrassed too.
wortfallen.cheveux.react: Long black body hair? Visit the hairdresser.
wortfallen.cheveux.tip: False friend for Spanish and Italian speakers (pelo) and Portuguese speakers (pelo, which also means hair on the body). Cheveux is the hair on your head (always plural). Poil is the hair on the body or an animal's fur.
wortfallen.pretendre.react: You claim to become a nurse? Prove it!
wortfallen.pretendre.tip: False friend for Spanish (pretender) and Portuguese (pretender) speakers, where it means to intend, and for English speakers (to pretend = faire semblant). French prétendre is to claim. To intend is avoir l'intention de, compter or vouloir.
wortfallen.fermer.react: A bus that does not close? Do the doors work?
wortfallen.fermer.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (fermare = to stop). French fermer is to close a door, a shop or a bank account. To stop is arrêter or s'arrêter.
wortfallen.camera.react: A film camera at the hotel? Where will you sleep?
wortfallen.camera.tip: False friend for Italian speakers (camera = room). French caméra is a video camera (a stills camera is un appareil photo). A room in a hotel or flat is une chambre (the sleeping room) or une pièce.
wortfallen.parents.react: All your parents? How many do you have?
wortfallen.parents.tip: False friend for Italian (parenti), Spanish (parientes) and Portuguese (parentes) speakers, where it means relatives. French les parents are mother and father. For all relatives, say la famille or les proches.
wortfallen.eventuellement.react: Possibly found one? Did you find it or not?
wortfallen.eventuellement.tip: False friend for English speakers (eventually). For German (eventuell) and Italian (eventualmente) it means the same as in French: possibly, in some cases. Eventually is finalement or à la fin.
wortfallen.pain.m2: to hurt, to be in pain
wortfallen.pain.react: Lots of bread in your back? Eat it, don't carry it.
wortfallen.pain.tip: False friend for English speakers (pain). Le pain is bread. Pain at the doctor's: j'ai mal au dos, j'ai mal à la tête, la douleur (noun).
wortfallen.coin.react: A corner of one euro? Which part?
wortfallen.coin.tip: False friend for English speakers (coin). Le coin is a corner: au coin de la rue. A coin is une pièce (de monnaie). Une pièce is also a room in a flat: un deux-pièces.
wortfallen.cave.react: A cellar with prehistoric drawings? Whose cellar?
wortfallen.cave.tip: False friend for English speakers (cave). A cave you visit is une grotte. La cave is the cellar under a building, where you store wine, bikes or boxes.
wortfallen.rude.react: A tough waiter? Did he arm-wrestle you?
wortfallen.rude.tip: False friend for English speakers (rude = impolite). French rude is harsh or hard: un hiver rude, une rude journée. Not polite is impoli, mal élevé or grossier.
wortfallen.sale.react: A dirty shop, at half price? Hmm.
wortfallen.sale.tip: False friend for English speakers (sale). Sale is dirty: une chemise sale. A sale with reductions is les soldes (the two official seasons are in winter and summer) or une promotion. Sale is used before a noun too: une sale histoire.
wortfallen.medecine.react: A whole medical science for a cough? Expensive!
wortfallen.medecine.tip: False friend for English, Spanish (medicina), Portuguese (medicina) and Italian (medicina) speakers. La médecine is the field or the practice. The pill or syrup is un médicament.
wortfallen.brave.react: Brave? Did he fight a dragon at school?
wortfallen.brave.tip: False friend for German speakers (brav = well-behaved). French brave after a noun is courageous: un pompier brave; before a noun it means decent: un brave type. For a child who behaves, French says sage: sois sage.

verben.title: The most important verbs
verben.mascot: You need these verbs every day.
verben.lead: A mini grammar to look things up: {n} verbs in every tense and mood, with avoir or être in the compound tenses. Whatever doesn't follow the pattern is <mark class="vb-x">highlighted</mark>: that's what you have to learn.
verben.group.hilfsverb.name: être, avoir, aller
verben.group.hilfsverb.what: The three verbs you need from day one. All three are irregular in almost every tense, and être and avoir build every compound tense.
verben.group.modal.name: Verb + infinitive
verben.group.modal.what: They say what is possible, wanted, necessary or known. A second verb follows, in the infinitive.
verben.group.unregelmaessig.name: Irregular verbs
verben.group.unregelmaessig.what: Each has its own forms, shown highlighted, but most fall into families you can learn together: prendre, comprendre, apprendre; venir, tenir, devenir.
verben.group.regelmaessig.name: Regular verbs
verben.group.regelmaessig.what: Take -er, -ir or -re off the infinitive and add the endings of the group. Nine verbs out of ten end in -er and work like parler, and new verbs do too.
verben.group.stem-change.name: Spelling-change -er verbs
verben.group.stem-change.what: Regular -er endings, but the stem changes its spelling to keep its sound. The changes are highlighted.
verben.group.trennbar.name: Pronominal verbs
verben.group.trennbar.what: Verb + reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se). The pronoun changes with the person: je me lève à sept heures, elle se lève à huit heures.
verben.when.subj: il faut que…, je veux que…

verben.practice.modal: Practise verb + infinitive: pouvoir, vouloir, devoir

lesen.a1-phone-messages.blurb: Four short messages: who wrote, and what do they want?
lesen.a2-padron-notice.blurb: An invented town's notice for practice. Every mairie has its own list, so check yours.
schreiben.a2-email-school.blurb: Your child is ill: say so clearly, and ask about the homework.
schreiben.a2-padron-form.blurb: A practice version of a form you may really meet. Every mairie has its own, so check yours.
schreiben.b1-email-landlord.blurb: The boiler has broken: describe the problem, ask for a date, stay polite.
schreiben.b1-email-employer.blurb: An appointment you can't move, a shift to swap: asking for something at work.
schreiben.b2-opinion-text.blurb: Take a position, give reasons, answer the other side – and end on a clear conclusion.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.0: “Prénom” is your first name; “nom” is your surname. Many French forms put the surname first (“Nom, prénom”). Read the labels, not the order in the text.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.1: The date is day/month/year: 04/03/1996. 03/04/1996 would be 3 April.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.2: “Code postal” and “commune” go in separate fields, even if they are together in the text. The number comes before the street: “12, rue de l'Orme”.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.3: Accents count: “natation”, “Ríos”, “débutante”. A woman writes “débutante”, a man “débutant”.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.0: All four points are there: in an exam, a missing point costs more than a small grammar mistake.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.1: There is a greeting and a sign-off (Salut Lucie, / Gros bisous).
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.2: French puts a non-breaking space before ? and !: “On se voit dimanche ?”, “Joyeux anniversaire !”. No space at all is the typical mistake.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.3: The sentences are short. At A1, “Je dois travailler.” is better than a long sentence with a mistake. Note “ne … pas” around the verb: “je ne peux pas venir”.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.0: The requests are questions (“Pourriez-vous… ?”, “Cela vous dérangerait-il de… ?”), not orders (“Arrosez mes plantes”, “Vous devez…”).
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.1: After “Cela vous dérangerait-il de…” comes the infinitive: “de relever mon courrier”.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.2: “Vous” all the way through: “je vous apporte”, “votre aide”, “pourriez-vous”. One “tu” in the middle would stand out.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.3: Greeting and sign-off match: “Bonjour Madame Ortega,” → “Cordialement,”. “Bises” is too familiar for a neighbour you hardly know. The greeting ends with a comma.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.0: “Il est malade” with “être”, or “il a de la fièvre” with “avoir”. “Il a malade” is a typical mistake.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.1: The teacher can tell at once which child and which class it is about. Schools usually also expect a written reason for an absence; this message does that job.
schreiben.check.a2-email-school.2: A polite question: “Pourriez-vous me dire… ?”. “Vous” is the safe choice in a first message to a teacher; there is no need to switch to “tu”, even if the teacher is friendly.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.0: Numbers are spoken, not written: “le vingt novembre mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-huit” → 20/11/1988. French phone numbers are said in pairs: “zéro six, trente-neuf, quatre-vingt-dix-huit, zéro trois, quinze” → 06 39 98 03 15.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.1: Careful with “Premier rendez-vous ?”. He answers “Non” to a different question (“Êtes-vous déjà venu ?”), so here the right answer is “oui”.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.2: “Parfait” means the appointment is confirmed, so fill in the doctor, the date and the time. “Quinze heures trente” is 15:30.
schreiben.check.a2-padron-form.0: A French address runs number, street, then floor and door: “5, rue des Prés, 1er étage, porte B”.
schreiben.check.a2-padron-form.1: “Commune précédente” asks where you lived before: Marseille, not Valdaure and not Tanger.
schreiben.check.a2-padron-form.2: Copy your document number exactly, digit by digit. The number here is a made-up example.
schreiben.check.a2-padron-form.3: This is language practice, not official guidance: the real form and the papers to bring vary, so ask at your own mairie.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.0: All four points are there, and the landlady can act on them: what is broken, since when, when someone can come.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.1: The tenses tell the story: “est tombée en panne lundi” (one event, passé composé) and “nous n'avons plus” after “depuis” (still true now, present tense).
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.2: “Vous” throughout, and a comma after the greeting: “Madame Lefèvre,”. “Chère Madame” is more personal than a first message to a landlady needs.
schreiben.check.b1-email-landlord.3: “Préférez-vous que je m'en charge” : “préférer que” takes the subjunctive.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.0: A solution comes with the request: the boss reads “je peux échanger mon service avec Jordi” and only has to say yes.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.1: “Tu” with your boss is normal in many French workplaces. If yours uses “vous”, keep to it: “Je vous écris pour vous demander un service”, “Pourriez-vous me répondre… ?”.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.2: The tone is a request, not an announcement: “Si cela te convient” softens it.
schreiben.check.b1-email-employer.3: Time off for official appointments depends on your contract and your collective agreement (“convention collective”); this task practises the email, not your rights.
schreiben.check.b2-beschwerde-reiseveran: No angry words: “J'ai le regret de vous informer que plusieurs problèmes graves se sont produits” instead of “c'est une honte”. At B2 the tone is part of the mark: firm, but never rude.
Each problem is set against a promise (“Votre brochure présentait… Or, il se trouvait en réalité…”). A complaint without that comparison is only an opinion.
There is a clear demand AND a deadline. Without a date, a letter of complaint is not complete.

B2 linking words and forms: “or”, “de plus”, “comme”, “donc”, “sans que” + subjunctive. The formal frame: “Madame, Monsieur,” at the top (with a comma) and the fixed closing formula “Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées” : it repeats the form of address you opened with.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.0: The position is clear in the first paragraph, and the last paragraph comes back to it.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.1: Each argument has an example of its own. “Il serait plus sûr” alone is a claim; the two busy streets on the way to school make it real.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.2: The other side gets a fair sentence before the answer: “Il est vrai que… ; cependant…”.
schreiben.check.b2-opinion-text.3: B2 forms: the conditional for what would happen (“améliorerait”, “gagnerait”), “il ne s'agit pas de…, mais de…”, “je préfère que” + subjunctive.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.0: Every field is filled in. An empty field counts as a mistake, even if the information is in the text.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.1: Copy names, numbers and dates exactly as they are in the text, with their accents; in France the day comes before the month (le 12 septembre, 12/09).
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.2: Nothing made up: if something is not in the text, leave the field empty or put a dash.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.0: Every point in the task is covered. A missing point costs more than three grammar mistakes.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.1: Greeting and sign-off suit each other and the person (Salut Théo, … À bientôt !).
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.2: The sentences are linked (donc, parce que, mais, de plus, même si), not just one after the other.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.0: Read first, then compare: discuss the text only once you have marked every mistake you can find.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.1: The text has about 15 mistakes. Look at: agreement and gender (“très sale”, “la problème”), prepositions after verbs and adjectives (“en colère sur”, “s'en intéresser”), adverb or adjective (“pas bon”), the subjunctive after “je voudrais que”, a missing article (“tous locataires”), a plural verb, a capital letter in a date, the space before “?”, and a closing line that is not a French formula.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.2: Write down the mistakes you make yourself, too. That is the point of the task.
satzmelodie.rule.cortes: A polite request is often a statement with je voudrais (the voice falls), or a question with pourriez-vous (the voice rises gently). s'il vous plaît and a friendly tone do the rest.

delesiele.title: DELF, TCF or TEF?
delesiele.lead: All three are serious French exams. What decides between them is what you need the result for: for Canada it is the TCF Canada or the TEF Canada, for a residence card or nationality it is an exam on the prefecture's list (TCF IRN, TEF IRN or a DELF/DALF), and for a diploma that never expires it is the DELF or DALF. For anything else, ask the institution first.

delesiele.tips.title: If you still can't decide
delesiele.tips.1: You don't know your level: the TCF and the TEF place you wherever you are, while a DELF at the wrong level can end in a fail.
delesiele.tips.2: You want a result that never runs out: the DELF and DALF diplomas have no expiry date as far as we could check, while a TCF or TEF result is valid for a limited time.
delesiele.tips.3: You need a result soon: TCF and TEF sessions are usually easier to book than DELF sessions. Check that the institution accepts it first.
delesiele.tips.4: You apply for Canada: take the Canada version of the TCF or the TEF. A DELF is not enough, and a general TCF or TEF may not be either.
delesiele.tips.5: You only know French as it is spoken in France: tests such as the TCF Canada and the TEF Canada can include Québec accents, so practise hearing them too.

delesiele.p.nationality.title: Residence card and French nationality
delesiele.p.nationality.answer: TCF IRN, TEF IRN or a DELF / DALF
delesiele.p.nationality.text: For a multi-year card, a resident card or naturalisation, the prefecture asks for proof of a French level. The level has changed over the years and depends on the procedure, so look at the current list on service-public.fr. In general, an exam from the list is accepted: the TCF IRN and the TEF IRN are made for exactly this, and a DELF or DALF at or above the level asked usually counts too. Results older than the validity period do not count, so don't book too early. Some people are exempt, for example because of a French diploma, so check your own case with the prefecture.
delesiele.p.university.title: University in France
delesiele.p.university.answer: Often DELF B2 / DALF, or TCF DAP: ask first
delesiele.p.university.text: Universities usually ask for B2, sometimes C1 for demanding courses, and each one names the exams it accepts. A DELF B2 or a DALF is a safe bet, and the TCF for admission to French universities (TCF DAP) is built for it. Some institutions also take the TCF tout public or the TEF. Get the rule in writing from the admissions office, including how old your result may be.
delesiele.p.work.title: Work and your CV
delesiele.p.work.text: Private employers care more about your level than about the exam. A DELF or DALF has no expiry date, which suits a CV. A TCF or TEF result is valid for a limited time, but it is quick to book if you need a result soon. Regulated professions and public jobs can have their own rules, so check the call or the professional body.
delesiele.p.visa.title: Visas, scholarships and other official uses
delesiele.p.visa.answer: Read the rules of the procedure
delesiele.p.visa.text: We can't give a general answer here. A consulate, ministry or scholarship body says which certificates it accepts, at which level, and how old they may be. If the rules name only one exam, take that one. This page is general orientation, not legal advice.
delesiele.p.self.title: For yourself
delesiele.p.self.text: If you want one level to work towards and a diploma at the end, the DELF or DALF fits. If you want to see where you stand, the TCF gives you a level on a six-step scale, and you don't have to know your level before you book.

nat.title: French residence card and nationality: language level and civic exam
nat.lead: To get a multi-year card, a resident card or French nationality, you now have to show a level of French and, from 2026, pass a civic exam. Here is which level each step asks for, who may be exempt and the steps to naturalisation in order.
nat.legal: General orientation, not legal advice. The levels below are the ones we understand to apply in November 2026, after the 2024 immigration law and the decrees that followed. We have not read every text, and we have not checked how each préfecture applies them. Everything marked “to verify” must be confirmed on service-public.fr or with your préfecture before you act.
nat.short.title: The short version
nat.short.1: For a first multi-year card, a first resident card and naturalisation, you must show a set level of French and pass the civic exam (to verify).
nat.short.2: The level rises with each step: A2, then B1, then B2 (to verify).
nat.short.3: You prove your level with an approved test, such as the TCF IRN, or with a French diploma. Some people are exempt.
nat.short.4: Naturalisation is a long procedure: an online application, an interview, a decision by decree and a ceremony.
nat.steps.title: Naturalisation by decree: the steps, in order
nat.s1.title: 1. Check that you can apply
nat.s1.text: You must be an adult and, as a general rule, have lived in France legally for five years. Shorter periods can apply, for example after studies in France (to verify). Your life must be centred in France, with a stable situation.
nat.s2.title: 2. Reach the language level and pass the civic exam
nat.s2.text: Take an approved language test and the civic exam. Centres have fixed dates and results take a while, so book early. You can practise with our TCF IRN mock and our civic exam pages.
nat.s3.title: 3. Collect your documents
nat.s3.text: Typically: identity and residence documents, your birth certificate (with a sworn translation if it is not in French), proof of address and income, tax notices, your language certificate and your civic exam result. The list changes, so use the one on the official site (to verify).
nat.s4.title: 4. Apply online
nat.s4.text: The application is filed online, on the platform for foreign nationals (ANEF), with scanned documents (to verify). Keep your confirmation.
nat.s5.title: 5. The interview
nat.s5.text: You are invited to an interview (the entretien d'assimilation) at the préfecture. The officer checks your French, your knowledge of France and its values, and your situation. Be ready to talk about your work, your family, your life in France and the principles of the Republic.
nat.s6.title: 6. Wait for the decision
nat.s6.text: The file is checked by the authorities, and this often takes a year or more (to verify). The decision is published as a decree. A refusal or a postponement can be challenged: get advice from a lawyer or an association.
nat.s7.title: 7. The ceremony
nat.s7.text: If the answer is yes, you are invited to a welcome ceremony. You become French from the date of the decree.
nat.s7.after: After that you can ask for a French identity card and passport. Whether your first country still treats you as its citizen depends on its own law, so ask its consulate.
nat.other: This page covers the language and civic steps for residence cards and naturalisation by decree. Nationality by marriage, by birth in France or through a parent has its own rules and conditions.

dgt.orient.title: The driving licence in France: a short orientation
dgt.orient.legal: General orientation, not legal advice. Rules, prices and exam details change, and we could not check every point. Treat this as a first picture and confirm it with a driving school (auto-école) or the official sites below.
dgt.orient.1: For a car licence (permis B) you pass a theory test (le code, officially l'examen du code de la route) and a practical driving test (l'épreuve pratique). Most people go through a driving school (auto-école); you can also register as an independent candidate (candidat libre).
dgt.orient.2: The theory test is taken on a screen at an approved exam centre. The number of questions, the timing and the pass mark change, so check the current format with your driving school or the official site. To verify.
dgt.orient.3: The test is in French. Whether another language or an interpreter is allowed depends on the current rules, so ask when you register. Signs, instructions and papers will be in French in any case. To verify.
dgt.orient.4: The application file is handled online through the ANTS (the national agency for secure titles); your driving school usually does it with you. A medical check applies to some drivers only. Check the current steps. To verify.
dgt.orient.5: If you already hold a licence from another country, you may be able to exchange it (échange de permis) instead of taking the tests. It depends on the country that issued it and on strict deadlines after you settle in France, so check yours with the ANTS or your préfecture first. To verify.

ap.hint.title.text: Learning gender through rules only takes you so far, because many rules have exceptions. What works best is learning every noun together with its article (la table, le livre, l'eau, which is feminine), for example in the vocabulary trainer, and then meeting the words in everyday life. Treat the rules as help with a new word. The most reliable ones: -tion and -sion → la, -ment and -isme → le. Careful with -age: le garage, but la plage and la page.
ap.regel.intro: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article usually shows which: le or la. Before a vowel or a mute h both become l', which hides the gender: l'école is feminine, l'hôtel masculine. The ending of the noun is often a good clue. These patterns help when you meet a new word, but they have exceptions, so learn each noun with its article.
ap.regel.people: With people the article usually follows the person: le boulanger / la boulangère, le journaliste / la journaliste. For many words there is no pattern at all, and the article simply has to be learned with the word.

delesiele.p.canada.title: Immigration to Canada
delesiele.p.canada.text: Canadian immigration programmes accept only specific tests, and they convert your scores into NCLC levels. Take the Canada version of the TCF or the TEF, not the general one and not a DELF. The points you get depend on the programme and the level, so read the current rules of the programme you apply to. Canadian accents are part of these tests, so listen to some Québec French as well.

Transitional rules, exceptions and the exact meaning of “first card” can differ in your case. Our practice material aims at a level, but it cannot predict a result.
nat.how.title: How you prove your level
nat.how.1: Take a test from an approved list at an accredited centre. The TCF IRN is made for residence and nationality. Other tests, such as the TEF for integration, residence and nationality, or the DELF and DALF diplomas, may also count (to verify which ones for which step).
nat.how.2: A certificate is valid for a limited time (often counted in two years) and the centre must be approved. Check the current list before you book.
nat.how.3: For naturalisation the test must cover speaking and writing as well as listening and reading (to verify).
nat.how.4: A diploma from French-language education may replace a test (to verify which ones). Ask which of your diplomas count.
nat.ex.title: Who may be exempt (to verify)
nat.ex.1: Exemptions exist, but they are narrow and depend on the step. The texts we saw mention people above a certain age (65 is the figure we found), people whose disability or health problem prevents them from taking the test, and people with certain statuses such as refugees. Details differ by step.
nat.ex.2: People who studied in France or in a French-language school may be able to show their level with that diploma instead of a test.
nat.ex.3: A medical certificate is usually part of an exemption request, and the authorities decide. Don't assume you are exempt: ask before you stop preparing.
nat.ex.4: Children and teenagers are treated differently from adults. This page is about adults.
nat.cir.title: On arrival: the OFII and the contrat d'intégration républicaine
nat.cir.1: When many newcomers receive their first long-stay permit, the OFII (Office français de l'immigration et de l'intégration) invites them to sign a contrat d'intégration républicaine (CIR). In it you promise to follow civic training and, if your French is low, language lessons, and you have an interview and a language test at the start (to verify the details).
nat.cir.2: The CIR is separate from the later steps in the table, but the French you learn there is your start towards A2. Keep your attendance certificates: they may be asked for later (to verify).

wissen.faq.where.q: Where can I download free French grammar PDFs?
wissen.faq.where.a: Here: one grammar book per level from A1 to C1 and one complete book, each with rules, tables, exercises and answers. They are free, with no account and no email address, and you may print them and share them in class.
wissen.faq.level.q: Which PDF is right for my level?
wissen.faq.level.a: If you are not sure, start with Grammar Start (A1–B1): the ten chapters you need first. Or take the free placement test on this site, which tells you your level. The word lists follow the same levels, A1 to C2.
wissen.faq.free.q: Are the PDFs really free? Can teachers use them in class?
wissen.faq.free.a: Yes. We wrote everything ourselves from this course's own material, so we can give it away. You may print the files and share them with your students. You may not sell them or publish them on other websites.
wissen.faq.official.q: Where can I find official sample papers for the DELF, DALF, TCF and TEF?
wissen.faq.official.a: The exam bodies publish them on their own websites: France Éducation international for the DELF, DALF and TCF, and the CCI Paris Île-de-France for the TEF. We do not copy them: we link to each page under “Official sample papers”, where they are always up to date.
wissen.faq.answers.q: Do the grammar books have answers?
wissen.faq.answers.a: Yes. Every exercise has lines to write on, and the answers are in a key (corrigé) at the back of the book. Each chapter also links to the same topic online, where your answers are checked right away.
